query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: When pre-passivated Q235 steel undergoes a controlled, gradual annealing treatment at 700–900 °C under a low-chloride, inert gas environment before salt exposure, the passive film transforms into a denser and more adherent Fe3+ oxide layer that enhances corrosion protection compared to unannealed samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel with its initial, uniform passivation film produced by industrial pickling and passivation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing protocol with a slow temperature ramp (e.g., 5 °C/min) to reach 800 °C and a 1-hour dwell in an inert atmosphere, followed by exposure to an aggressive salt environment.
generation.conditions: Annealing at 700–900 °C with a controlled ramp rate under inert (e.g., argon) conditions, then salt exposure at high temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thermally transformed, dense Fe3+ oxide layer replacing or modifying the original passivation film.
generation.mechanism: Gradual heating minimizes thermal stresses while providing sufficient energy for the passivation film to re-crystallize into a stoichiometrically stable Fe3+ oxide (such as Fe2O3) that is more compact and adherent, thus better resisting salt-induced corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed samples will exhibit lower corrosion weight loss and superior protective film integrity (evidenced by higher impedance in EIS tests and denser oxide morphology in SEM) compared to unannealed, rapidly heated samples.
generation.baseline: Passivated Q235 steel samples that are exposed directly to salt environments without the controlled, gradual annealing step.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the heating rate is sufficiently low; too rapid heating would negate the densification effect, leading instead to film rupture.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal ramp rate and dwell time for achieving the protective film transformation without inducing stresses remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare corrosion behavior of two sets of passivated Q235 steel: one subjected to controlled gradual annealing (5 °C/min ramp to 800 °C, 1 hr dwell under argon) and one subjected to rapid heating to the same temperature. Both sets are then exposed to identical salt spray conditions at high temperature. Perform EIS, weight loss measurements, and microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM) of the oxide film.
measurements: XRD phase identification and SEM morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the gradually annealed samples do not show significantly improved corrosion resistance and denser, more protective oxide films compared to the rapid-heating sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: However, it is noteworthy that the Cr-rich oxide scale is not observed in the sectional distribution diagram of the elements in the S0 sample without Si, which may have resulted from the destruction of the Cr-rich oxide scale generated previously, and the high-temperature corrosion resistance of the cladding layer that mainly comes from the rapid formation of a Cr2O3 oxide film to hinder the continuation of the reaction. The selective oxidation of the surface occurred firstly in high-temperature thermal corrosion, and the Cr-rich oxide scale was destroyed. O, S and Cl diffused into the cladding layer due to the destruction of the Cr-rich oxide scale, resulting in severely accelerated corrosion. When the surface oxide scale was mainly composed of NiO, oxidation corrosion was aggravated as the acid melting and fusing reaction of NiO and Na2SO4 occurred, so that the weight loss of the Ni-Cr-Mo cladding layer without Si in thermal corrosion was much greater than that of the Ni-Cr-Mo cladding layer with Si added, and increased significantly at later stages.

In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.

papers.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.
papers.system: Q235 low‐carbon (pipeline) steel with an industrial pickled–passivated surface
papers.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion tests with macroscopic, microscopic, weight loss, and EDS analysis
papers.findings: Identified four stages from initial passivation film formation through its local shedding, widespread film rupture, substrate rust formation, and finally, the development of a loosely bonded, bulging mixed rust layer; the film initially retards corrosion due to its electrochemical protection but later fails as chloride ions infiltrate cracks.
papers.mechanism: The protective passivation film initially limits electrochemical reactions; under aggressive salt spray, film residues mix with newly formed rust, creating stress concentrations and cracks that allow further corrosive attack. Elemental shifts (e.g., decrease in fluorine and increase in oxygen) accompany the transition from passivation product to iron oxide-based rust.

papers.title: The Effect of Temperatures on the Passivation Behavior of Q235 Steel in the Simulated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel immersed in simulated concrete pore (SCP) solution
papers.approach: Passivation experiments at controlled temperatures (20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C) with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and XPS analysis
papers.findings: Demonstrated a two-stage passivation process (rapid formation within 24 h and then a stable phase) where increased temperature accelerates film formation and alters film composition (with more Fe3+ compounds such as Fe2O3), resulting in films with enhanced impedance and improved protective properties.
papers.mechanism: Temperature influences the kinetics and composition of the passive film. At higher temperatures, the rapid growth of a thicker, more stable oxide film (rich in Fe3+ species) improves corrosion resistance, suggesting that thermal activation can enhance passivation if the film remains adherent and intact.

papers.title: High-Temperature Corrosion of Ni-Cr-Mo Cladding Layers with Different Si Contents in NaCl-KCl-Na2SO4-K2SO4
papers.system: Q235 steel substrate with laser-cladded Ni-Cr-Mo alloy layers (with varying Si content)
papers.approach: High-temperature (550 °C) salt exposure with weight loss measurements, XRD, and SEM analysis to assess phase formation and oxide scale integrity
papers.findings: Found that adding Si improves corrosion resistance by facilitating formation of a denser, protective Cr-rich oxide layer. In samples without Si, the oxide scale was destroyed, allowing aggressive species (O, S, Cl) to penetrate, thereby accelerating corrosion.
papers.mechanism: The formation and stability of a protective oxide scale (largely Cr2O3) are critical at high temperatures; alloying elements (like Si) modify the film’s density and adherence. Although the study used coatings, it underscores the importance of stable oxide film chemistry for high-temperature protection.

papers.title: Effective Corrosion Inhibition of Carbon Steel in Hydrochloric Acid by Dopamine-Produced Carbon Dots.
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in 1 M HCl solution
papers.approach: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, weight loss measurements, and surface analysis following treatment with nitrogen-doped carbon dots (NCDs) as inhibitors
papers.findings: Observed high inhibition efficiencies (up to roughly 96%) with increasing NCD concentration and exposure time – indicating that the formation of an adsorbed inhibitor film effectively slows acidic corrosion.
papers.mechanism: NCDs adsorb onto the steel surface, creating a barrier that obstructs corrosive species. Adsorption follows the Langmuir isotherm, suggesting a uniform film coverage that retards corrosion reactions.

papers.title: Study on Synergistic Corrosion Inhibition Effect between Calcium Lignosulfonate (CLS) and Inorganic Inhibitors on Q235 Carbon Steel in Alkaline Enviro
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in alkaline (pH 11.5) solutions with and without hybrid inhibitor systems
papers.approach: Electrochemical (open circuit potential, polarization, impedance) and microscopic (SEM) characterization to assess the effect of pre-filming and inhibitor adsorption
papers.findings: Demonstrated that pre-filming with inhibitors such as CLS (combined with molybdate, stannate or tungstate) leads to the formation of a multi-layer protective film, significantly increasing resistance and reducing pitting susceptibility compared to untreated steel.
papers.mechanism: The inhibitor system forms a complex film (comprising passivation, deposition, and adsorption layers) that enhances the re-passivation ability and blocks corrosive ions. The molybdate component is particularly effective in promoting a higher re-passivation potential.

established: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state exhibits a protective passivation film that can initially retard corrosion via an electrochemical barrier effect.
Temperature and environmental exposure significantly influence both the kinetics of passivation film formation and its subsequent degradation in corrosive environments.
The integrity and composition of the passive/oxide layer (including species such as Fe2O3 or Cr-rich oxides in modified systems) are pivotal for controlling corrosion rates.

approaches_tried.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion testing
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified sequential stages of film breakdown and substrate rust formation; initial protection is lost due to film rupture and chloride ingress.

approaches_tried.approach: Temperature-controlled passivation experiments in simulated pore solution
approaches_tried.outcome: Higher temperatures accelerate passivation film formation and affect composition, suggesting improved early-stage protection if the film remains intact.

approaches_tried.approach: Application of organic/inorganic inhibitor additives (e.g., NCDs, CLS hybrids)
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced corrosion inhibition via formation of adsorbed films that reduce active corrosion sites, although studies have focused primarily on room-temperature acid or alkaline conditions rather than high temperature.

mechanisms: Integrity and adhesion of the passivation/oxide film controlling barrier properties
Temperature-driven acceleration of film formation and compositional transformations (e.g., increased Fe3+ oxide content)
Film rupture due to mechanical stress from volumetric changes, chloride ion attack, or mismatched thermal expansion at high temperatures
Adsorption of inhibitor species (organic or inorganic) that restore or mimic passivation behavior
disagreements: Some studies emphasize chloride ion ingress and mechanical rupture as the primary trigger for film breakdown, while others point to temperature-induced phase transformation and compositional shifts as the dominant factors.

There is disagreement over whether high-temperature environments universally degrade the protective film or whether, under certain conditions (e.g., with alloying or inhibitor compounds), high temperatures can enhance film stability.
open_questions: For pre-exposed (passivated) Q235 steel, what is the dominant failure mechanism when transitioning from room temperature to high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure conditions?
How does the pre-existing oxide/passivation film transform under high-temperature thermal cycling, and what compositional changes lead to either retained protection or accelerated degradation?
Can a controlled annealing study isolate the role of thermal-induced film rupture versus compositional transformation in determining corrosion outcomes?
opportunities: Conduct a controlled study where pre-passivated Q235 steel samples are subjected to annealing at 700–900 °C in a well-defined salt atmosphere (with and without chloride aggressive species) to isolate thermal effects.
Compare treated (inhibitor-modified or alloy-coated) versus untreated Q235 samples to establish reference behaviors in both room-temperature and high-temperature regimes.

Utilize combined electrochemical (EIS, polarization), weight loss, and surface analytical techniques (EDS, XPS) pre- and post-annealing to correlate film composition changes with corrosion resistance.

Investigate if implementations from HEA cladding research (e.g., alloying elements promoting stable high-temperature oxide films) can be integrated with pre-exposure treatments to enhance thermal corrosion protection.

directions.direction: Investigate the microstructural transformation of the pre-formed passivation film on Q235 steel during high‐temperature exposure (700–900 °C) by monitoring phase changes and film densification.
directions.assessment: Directly targets how the oxide film’s composition evolves under high temperature. Evidence from studies on temperature‐accelerated passivation (e.g. PMC9867134) supports that higher temperatures lead to different iron oxide phases. Feasible with XRD, XPS and electron microscopy.

directions.direction: Assess the influence of thermal-mechanical stress (thermal expansion mismatch) on film integrity, leading to microcrack formation and subsequent chloride ingress.
directions.assessment: Explicitly tests whether the pre-passivated film breaks apart due to thermal cycling. Supported by observations of film rupture and spallation (PMC9504384). Feasible with in-situ high-temperature microscopy and stress analysis.

directions.direction: Conduct controlled salt exposure experiments comparing abrupt versus gradual heating protocols to isolate the effect of temperature ramp rate on film adherence and corrosion performance.
directions.assessment: Aims to establish whether controlled annealing can transform the passive film into a denser, more protective oxide layer. This approach is informed by temperature effects on passivation (PMC9867134) and is experimentally tractable.

directions.direction: Use electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at room and high temperatures to monitor the integrity and barrier properties of the passivation film under salt attack.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses electrical properties and barrier performance changes as the film transforms or cracks under high-temperature insult. Although high-temperature EIS is challenging, it is supported by room-temperature corrosion insights (PMC8226475) and provides quantitative measures.

directions.direction: Develop computational models to simulate thermal expansion mismatch effects between the steel substrate and the passivation film, predicting crack initiation and ion transport pathways.
directions.assessment: Complements experimental work by offering predictive insights into stress distributions and cracking. It can help identify parameter windows for failure but is less direct in isolating the mechanism without experimental validation.

Limited direct reference to experiments on Q235 steel at 700–900 °C under inert conditions.
fixes: Clarify which iron oxide phases predominate and validate with XRD analysis.
Cite prior thermal-oxidation data for Q235 or similar low-carbon steels to confirm the proposed oxide transformation.
evidence_needs: In-situ or ex-situ characterization (XRD, TEM) confirming oxide-phase evolution in Q235 steel during controlled annealing.
Comparative data on oxide layers formed under different heating rates and atmospheres.

minor_issues: Proposed mechanism references Cr-rich oxide protection from Ni-Cr-Mo systems, which may not fully transfer to Q235 carbon steel.
Less detail on the exact oxide composition formed under the slow heating vs. rapid heating scenarios.
fixes: Focus on Fe-based oxide scale formation relevant to Q235 steel composition rather than Ni-Cr-Mo alloys.
Provide more detailed phase confirmation (e.g., Fe2O3 vs. Fe3O4) and microstructural analysis.
evidence_needs: Direct experimental correlation of heating rate with oxide integrity in plain-carbon steels under salt exposure.
Data on the effect of moderate vs. high chloride environments on oxide stability for Q235.

minor_issues: Interchangeable use of 'Fe3+ oxide' without specifying whether Fe2O3 or Fe3O4 forms primarily.
Possibly underemphasizes the role of oxygen partial pressure in determining oxide phases.
fixes: Clarify the expected crystal structure(s) using references or succinct preliminary data (e.g., XRD).
Indicate how partial pressure of oxygen in the inert atmosphere is controlled.
evidence_needs: Experimental data on the transformation of passivation films into stable oxide scales on Q235 under controlled inert annealing.
Quantitative measurement of any difference in oxide thickness, composition, and adhesion between control and test samples.

minor_issues: Exact critical chloride threshold for initiating microcrack-assisted pitting remains unspecified.
Limited discussion on how to distinguish purely thermal microcracks from other cracking modes (e.g., mechanical damage).
fixes: Provide measured or literature-based estimates of the chloride threshold concentration.
Include a method (e.g., in-situ monitoring) to confirm that microcracking is thermally induced rather than from mechanical factors.
evidence_needs: Data from controlled thermal cycling experiments identifying microcrack formation thresholds in Q235 passivation layers.
Surface characterization methods (SEM/EBSD or XRD) to link microcrack induction to corrosion pit formation.

minor_issues: Direct comparison of high-temperature rapid heating to room-temperature salt exposure does not fully isolate high-temperature effects from purely chemical ones.
Potential oversimplification of the interplay between thermal stress and chloride-driven corrosion.
fixes: Add an intermediate heating-rate control to confirm that rapid heating (rather than simply higher temperature) is the cause of microcrack formation.
Detail the time–temperature profile needed to produce spallation and show how it is measured or modeled.
evidence_needs: In-situ high-temperature imaging or mechanical analysis of passivated steel to confirm thermal expansion mismatch as the key cause of film failure.
Comparative data between multiple heating rates and salt concentrations to confirm the synergy of temperature ramp and chloride.

fixes: Include references or preliminary data that demonstrate the formation of a dense and adherent Fe3+ oxide layer under the specified annealing conditions.

evidence_needs: Experimental studies or literature that confirm the formation of a dense Fe3+ oxide layer on Q235 steel under similar annealing conditions.
